clue.text: The left has had its say on the Canal

parts.note: port is the left-hand side of a ship
said means spoke or had its say

explanation.surface: A political left wing has spoken out about a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The left' reads as politics, but it is the nautical left. The definition is a description: the place lies on the Suez Canal, at its northern (Mediterranean) end.
explanation.definitionFit: This Egyptian port city sits at the Mediterranean mouth of the Suez waterway.

parts.note: Macaulay writes of a craftsman at his wheel; the wheel is a throwing wheel for clay, not a ship's or car's

explanation.surface: A driver or helmsman in Macaulay's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man at the wheel' suggests a helmsman; the wheel is the one on which clay is thrown, turning out pots.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of pots, bowls and jugs shapes clay on a spinning wheel.

explanation.surface: A sailor angrily joins in mocking someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a sailor; it is a roasting jack, the turning spit before a fire, which cooks meat over the heat. To roast someone is also to mock them harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: A spit-jack cooks meat by fierce heat before the fire, and harsh public mockery is a grilling.

parts.note: a second volume might be a follow-up work continuing the story of the first

explanation.surface: A second book in a series.
explanation.definitionFit: A book that continues the story of an earlier one follows it, as a second volume follows the first.

parts.note: recalls Tennyson's Locksley Hall: 'In the spring a livelier iris changes on the burnished dove', the spring colours shimmering on its neck

explanation.surface: A springtime dove with gleaming feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vernal' means of the spring; Tennyson's iris, the rainbow sheen on the dove's neck, gives the adjective, which comes from Iris the rainbow goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing shimmering rainbow colours that shift with the light, as a pigeon's neck does.

explanation.surface: Political deviationists enjoy themselves enormously.
explanation.walkthrough: In biology a sport is an organism that deviates abruptly from its type, a mutant; to sport is also to play or frolic.
explanation.definitionFit: Biological mutants departing from the parent type are called sports, and to sport is to frolic and play.

parts.note: a letter from a pastor to his flock has this name, which is also the title of Beethoven's Sixth Symphony

explanation.surface: Wondering about correspondence written by the composer.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop's letter to the clergy and people of the diocese is a pastoral letter; Beethoven's Sixth Symphony is the Pastoral.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastor's letter to his flock is so called, and the adjective names Beethoven's countryside symphony.

explanation.surface: A revealing exchange of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telling' looks like an adjective, 'revealing'; it is the noun, the act of narrating a story.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of narrating a story is a recounting, and a connection or correspondence between things is also so named.

clue.text: One never expects to be taken in by it

definitions.text: One never expects to be taken in by it

parts.words: One never expects to be taken in by it
parts.note: being taken by something unforeseen; it is by definition not expected

explanation.surface: Nobody anticipates being deceived by this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in' suggests deceived, but one is taken by this, caught unawares, precisely because it was not expected.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unexpected catches people off guard: an unforeseen event or shock.

parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Othello's speech in Act 3 begins 'O now, for ever / Farewell the ... mind! farewell content!' and the missing adjective fills the blank

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Othello with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello, convinced of Desdemona's infidelity, bids goodbye to his peace of mind; the solver supplies the word for calm.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Othello's lament describes a calm, untroubled mind at peace.

clue.text: Hewn stone in a setting of ash, larch and birch

indicators.note: the word sits inside the setting formed by the neighbouring tree names, so its letters run across them

explanation.surface: A dressed block of stone placed among ash, larch and birch trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and birch' only completes the woodland picture; the stone runs across 'ash, larch'.
explanation.definitionFit: Squared, dressed masonry blocks used for facing walls are called by this builder's term.

clue.text: It's not meet that they should!

definitions.text: It's not meet that they should!

parts.words: It's not meet that they should!
parts.note: plays on the proverb that opposite ends of a scale meet, with 'meet' read in its old sense of fitting or proper

explanation.surface: A prim objection that something would be improper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meet' looks like the archaic adjective for proper, but the proverb says these things meet; the clue grumbles that such a meeting is not seemly.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that utmost opposites end up touching, the furthest limits at either end.

parts.note: Nobody is the title character of The Diary of a Nobody, the Grossmiths' comic diary of a London clerk, whose weekly entries include Saturdays

explanation.surface: A complaint that nobody turns up at the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nobody' looks like 'no one', but it is the Nobody of the Diary, Charles the City clerk of The Laurels, Holloway, whose daily entries are headed by weekday.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles, the hapless clerk who writes The Diary of a Nobody, gives his surname to self-important suburban fussiness.

clue.text: Not very civil, so it can't be from the Duke!

definitions.text: Not very civil, so it can't be from the Duke!

parts.words: Not very civil, so it can't be from the Duke!
parts.note: a duke is addressed as Your Grace, so a remark lacking grace cannot have come from His Grace

explanation.surface: A rude message that surely was not sent by the Duke.
explanation.walkthrough: Dukes are styled 'Your Grace' in Britain, so something graceless cannot be his.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude and lacking courtesy or kindness, without grace in manner.

clue.text: Such goings-on in the drama school?

definitions.text: Such goings-on in the drama school?

parts.words: Such goings-on in the drama school?
parts.note: the drama school is Sheridan's play The School for Scandal, so goings-on there would be of that disgraceful kind

explanation.surface: Wondering about shocking behaviour at an academy for actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drama school' reads as a stage academy; it is the comedy The School for Scandal, by Sheridan.
explanation.definitionFit: Shocking, disgraceful conduct is what gossip feeds on, and this adjective describes it.

parts.note: cavalier here means a gallant gentleman attending a lady, not offhand or dismissive

explanation.surface: Behaved in a careless, offhand way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cavalier' suggests arrogance; in its older sense a cavalier is a lady's gallant attendant, who accompanies her.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallant who accompanied a lady as her attendant guarded and accompanied her.

clue.text: The little Spanish chestnut is a rattling good sort

definitions.text: The little Spanish chestnut is a rattling good sort

parts.words: The little Spanish chestnut is a rattling good sort
parts.note: the Spanish word for chestnut, castana, gives the name of the clicking instrument, which rattles in a dancer's hands

explanation.surface: A small Spanish chestnut praised as a fine fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rattling good sort' sounds like old slang for a fine chap; the instrument literally rattles, and its name comes from castaña, Spanish for chestnut, which its shape resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pair of wooden shells clicked in the hand by flamenco dancers, named from chestnut in Spanish.

clue.text: Hardly the vessel to dress overall

definitions.text: Hardly the vessel to dress overall

parts.words: Hardly the vessel to dress overall
parts.note: dressing a ship overall means hanging flags stem to stern; the vessel is Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS, whose name is also a sleeveless overall dress

explanation.surface: A ship unlikely to be decked out in flags.
explanation.walkthrough: HMS Pinafore is Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera ship; the word also names an overall-style dress, so it is hardly the vessel for dressing overall.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless apron-like garment worn over clothes, and the name of the comic opera ship of Gilbert and Sullivan.

parts.note: pictures rail passengers with newspapers at the station, while also describing sellers of paper and writing supplies

explanation.surface: Train travellers reading their newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Commuters who wait at stations might be called station-ers; the real word means dealers in paper, pens and envelopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Shopkeepers who sell writing paper, envelopes and pens are known by this trade name.

parts.note: a gap-fill from Gray's Elegy, where the owl complains of wanderers who 'near her secret bower, / ... her ancient solitary reign'

explanation.surface: A line from Gray's Elegy with its first word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' the moping owl complains of those who disturb her ancient solitary reign; the missing verb means disturb.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb in Gray's line means to disturb or trouble the owl's lonely domain.

parts.note: Abram, later Abraham, came from Ur of the Chaldees, so making for his town is heading to Ur

explanation.surface: Journeying towards the home town of Abram.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as ON TO UR: Abram, later Abraham, came from the Mesopotamian city of Ur.
explanation.definitionFit: Performers or teams away from home on a circuit of engagements are travelling.

clue.text: Like the first Mrs. Soames Forsyte ?

definitions.text: Like the first Mrs. Soames Forsyte ?

parts.words: Like the first Mrs. Soames Forsyte ?
parts.note: Soames's first wife in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga is named Irene, and the adjective sounds as if it means 'like her'

explanation.surface: Asking what Soames Forsyte's first wife was like.
explanation.walkthrough: Irene is Soames's first wife in Galsworthy's The Forsyte Saga; the adjective means peaceable, from Greek eirene, peace, the root of her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Peaceable and conciliatory, aiming at reconciliation, from the Greek word for peace.

clue.text: Initial cost of free-range eggs perhaps

parts.note: free-range hens lay their eggs out of doors

explanation.surface: The starting price of buying eggs from free-range hens.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as OUT LAY: free-range hens lay outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Money spent at the start of a venture is expenditure, the sum paid out.

clue.text: For a long drink on the Hesperus

definitions.text: For a long drink on the Hesperus

parts.words: For a long drink on the Hesperus
parts.note: two senses: a tall glass for sherry or beer, and the kind of sailing ship the Hesperus was in Longfellow's ballad

explanation.surface: Ordering a long drink aboard a ship called the Hesperus.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's 'The Wreck of the Hesperus' opens 'It was the schooner Hesperus'; the same word names a tall glass for beer or sherry.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-masted fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessel shares its name with a large beer or sherry glass.

parts.note: the sinew at the back of the heel is named after Achilles, and such a band is the body's own string, as in hamstring

explanation.surface: A Greek-themed string orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'string band' suggests a group of fiddlers; it is a fibrous cord, the one named after Achilles, whose heel was his weak spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough fibrous cord joining muscle to bone, like the one at the heel named after Achilles.

clue.text: Tiara'd lady at cards is fab !

definitions.text: Tiara'd lady at cards is fab

parts.words: Tiara'd lady at cards is fab
parts.note: two senses: the legendary woman said to have worn the papal tiara, and an old card game, with 'fab' short for fabulous, that is legendary

explanation.surface: A woman in a tiara playing cards is wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fab' is not slang praise but 'fabulous' in its root sense, belonging to fable: the female pontiff is a medieval legend. The name is also a Victorian card game.
explanation.definitionFit: A legendary female pontiff of the Middle Ages also names an old round game played with cards.

clue.text: The line is broken and scattered

explanation.surface: A broken line of things strewn about.
explanation.walkthrough: A broken line on a form is made of points; things scattered here and there are also described by the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A line made of points with gaps is broken, and objects strewn sparsely about are spread out.

indicators.note: the answer is made of the letters of the phrase, rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: The secret of an ice house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is the only signal: the answer is made from the letters of ICE STORE, which shuffle into the word for secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowledge understood only by an initiated few is arcane or private.
